concept.name: Liquidity sweep
concept.definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a run through a level where resting orders cluster — stop-losses and breakout entries just beyond an obvious high or low — followed by failure to hold beyond it: price trades through, fills those orders, and closes back inside the prior range. The same chart event is called a false breakout in classical TA; 'sweep' adds an interpretation (order collection) that a chart cannot prove.
concept.intuition: Price pokes through an obvious level, triggers the crowd's stops, then snaps back — the level was the target of the move, not an obstacle in its way.
concept.mechanics: Identification is a two-part check: mark pools where stops cluster (prior swing highs/lows, equal highs/lows, session extremes), then require the failure — a trade through the level (often on a wick) followed by a close back inside the old range. A close that holds beyond the level with continuation is a breakout, not a sweep.
concept.failure_modes: At the moment of the break a sweep and a genuine breakout are indistinguishable — only the close and follow-through separate them, so acting early means sometimes fading real breakouts.
concept.misconceptions: That sweeps prove a market maker deliberately hunted retail stops; order-flow research documents stop clustering at predictable levels, but intent is narrative, not observable fact.
concept.example: Price wicks above a prior swing high where buy stops rest, immediately rejects, and closes back inside the range; SMC traders read the level as swept and look for short setups on the retrace.
